channel.title: AI Stupa Translation Project
channel.description: New English translations of texts from the Tibetan Buddhist canon, made by the AI Stupa (provisional, public domain).

item.title: Praise of the Glorious Goddess Sarasvatī (Toh 1092)
item.description: Praise of the Glorious Goddess Sarasvatī, known in Tibetan as Pal Lhamo Drayang la Töpa, is a short devotional hymn addressed to Sarasvatī, the goddess of speech, learning, and eloquence, whom Tibetans call Yangchenma or Drayangma. It opens by taking refuge in the many maṇḍalas of wisdom through which the buddhas arise and the bodhisattva grounds unfold. It then praises Sarasvatī as a sage who…

item.title: The Noble Great Sūtra on Entering the City of Vaiśālī (Toh 1093)
item.description: The Noble Great Sūtra on Entering the City of Vaiśālī, known in Sanskrit as the Āryavaiśālīpraveśamahāsūtra and in Tibetan as Pakpa Yangpé Drongkhyer du Jukpé Do Chenpo, is a short discourse set during the Buddha's travels through the land of the Vṛjis. After staying at a boatmen's lodging among the reeds, the Buddha comes to Āmrapālī's grove outside Vaiśālī and sends the venerable Ānanda into…

item.title: The Aspiration Found in the Ritual Manual of Noble Avalokiteśvara (Toh 1094)
item.description: The Aspiration Found in the Ritual Manual of Noble Avalokiteśvara, the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel, known in Tibetan as Phakpa Chenrezik Wangchuk Yishin gyi Norbü Tokpa le Mönlam Jungwa, is a short aspiration prayer said to be drawn from a larger ritual manual devoted to Avalokiteśvara in his wish-fulfilling jewel form; no Sanskrit title is clearly attested for it. It opens with homage to the buddha…

item.title: The Noble King of Aspiration Prayers for Excellent Conduct (Toh 1095)
item.description: The Noble King of Aspiration Prayers for Excellent Conduct, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Bhadracaryāpraṇidhānarāja and in Tibetan as Pakpa Zangpo Chöpé Mönlam gyi Gyalpo, is one of the most beloved prayers in the Mahāyāna tradition. Written in verse and opening with homage to the youthful Mañjuśrī, it voices the bodhisattva's vast aspiration. It begins by bowing to all the buddhas of the three…

item.title: The Aspiration of Supreme Conduct (Toh 1097)
item.description: The Aspiration of Supreme Conduct, known in Sanskrit as Agracaryāpraṇidhāna and in Tibetan as Chokgi Chöpé Mönlam, is a short verse prayer of aspiration in the Mahāyāna tradition. It opens with an homage to all buddhas and bodhisattvas and bows to the buddhas of the ten directions for the benefit and happiness of all beings. It invokes Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and Dharmamati as models of how to pay…

item.title: The Jewel Verses (Toh 1098)
item.description: This short verse text, recorded in the Tibetan canon without a formal title and known by its theme as a discourse on the supreme jewels, is a poem of blessing and protection closely parallel to the Jewel Discourse, the Ratana Sutta of the Pali tradition, which is called the Ratnasūtra in Sanskrit. It opens with homage to the Three Jewels and then praises, verse by verse, the Buddha as the god of…

item.title: Toh 1099 (Toh 1099)
item.description: This short Kangyur text has no formal title of its own and is known by its opening words, "Homage to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones," in Tibetan Sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das rnams la phyag 'tshal. It is a brief verse prayer of auspiciousness and protection. It first recalls the seven buddhas of the past, from Vipaśyin through Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa to Śākyamuni…

item.title: Verses of Auspiciousness Requested by a God (Toh 1100)
item.description: Verses of Auspiciousness Requested by a God, known in Sanskrit as Devaparipṛcchāmaṅgalagāthā and in Tibetan as Lhas zhus pa'i bkra shis kyi tshigs su bcad pa, is a short verse text in which a god approaches the Buddha while he dwells in a solitary place and asks what the supreme auspiciousness is, since gods and humans each speak of auspicious things in their own way. In reply, the Buddha lists…

item.title: Verses of Well-Being (Toh 1101)
item.description: The Verses of Well-Being, known in Sanskrit as Svastigāthā and in Tibetan as Delek kyi Tsik su Chepa, is a brief verse text of blessing meant to be recited for auspiciousness and protection. It opens with a god approaching the Buddha and asking what words should be spoken so that well-being may arise, and the Buddha answers with a series of verses praising the Three Jewels as incomparable…

item.title: Verses for Well-Being (Toh 1102)
item.description: The Verses for Well-Being, known in Sanskrit as the Svastyayanagāthā and in Tibetan as Bde legs su 'gyur ba'i tshigs su bcad pa, is a brief scripture in verse that presents a dialogue between a god and the Buddha. The god approaches the Guide of the World and asks how one may always come to well-being, and the Buddha answers with a series of stanzas, each ending with the refrain that such people…

item.title: Verses of Auspiciousness (Toh 1103)
item.description: Verses of Auspiciousness, known in Sanskrit as Maṅgalagāthā and in Tibetan as Tashi kyi tsik su chepa, is a short work of benediction verses that celebrates the auspiciousness of the Three Jewels. After an opening homage, it praises the Buddha in turn as a golden mountain of excellence and protector of the three worlds, the sacred Dharma he taught as the supreme and unshakable virtue of the…

item.title: The King of Tantras (Toh 362)
item.description: The King of Tantras, the Glorious Kālacakra, Issued from the Supreme Primordial Buddha, known in Sanskrit as the Paramādibuddhoddhṛta Śrī Kālacakra Nāma Tantrarāja and in Tibetan as mchog gi dang po'i sangs rgyas las phyung ba rgyud kyi rgyal po dpal dus kyi 'khor lo, is the root scripture of the Kālacakra, or "Wheel of Time," tradition. It opens with King Sucandra bowing before the Buddha…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī That Saves the Preta Jvālāmukha (Toh 1080)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī That Saves the Preta Jvālāmukha, known in Tibetan as Yi dgas kha nas me 'bar ba la skyabs mdzad pa'i gzungs, is a short dhāraṇī scripture whose Sanskrit title is associated with the name of the flame-mouthed hungry ghost, Jvālāmukha. It opens with the Buddha teaching in Kapilavastu, while the venerable Ānanda, meditating alone at night, is confronted by a terrifying preta whose mouth…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī Called Obstructing Generosity (Toh 1081)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī Called Obstructing Generosity is a short scripture whose title is given only in Tibetan, with no Sanskrit title recorded, which suggests it may have been composed or compiled in Tibet rather than translated from an Indian original. After paying homage to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, it warns that obstructing the generosity of others brings consequences even worse than stinginess…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī for Giving Away the Body's Outflows as an Act of Generosity (Toh 1082)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for Giving Away the Body's Outflows is a brief ritual text in which the bodily excretions, including saliva, phlegm, nasal mucus, the dirt of the body, excrement, and urine, are offered as an act of generosity to the beings who feed on them. It opens with homage to the Three Jewels and gives a short mantra for each substance, instructing the practitioner to wish that those who eat…

item.title: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called the Seven Vetālas (Toh 1083)
item.description: The Noble Dhāraṇī Called the Seven Vetālas, known in Sanskrit as the Āryasaptavetāḍaka nāma dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as the Phakpa Rolang Dünpa, is a short protective scripture set on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, where the Buddha is staying with a great assembly of monks and his attendant Ānanda. Non-Buddhist ascetics send seven great vetālas, reanimated corpse-spirits, to harm the Buddha…

item.title: The Noble Heart of Gaṇapati (Toh 1084)
item.description: The Noble Heart of Gaṇapati, known in Sanskrit as Āryagaṇapatihṛdaya and in Tibetan as Pakpa Tsokkyi Dakpö Nyingpo, is a short dhāraṇī text centered on Gaṇapati, the Lord of the Hosts, a figure better known in wider Indian tradition as Gaṇeśa. Set on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, where the Buddha is accompanied by a great assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, it records the Buddha telling…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī Called Glorious Mahākāla (Toh 1085)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī Called Glorious Mahākāla, the Protector, known in Sanskrit as Śrī Mahākāla Nāma Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Dpal mgon po nag po zhes bya ba'i gzungs, is a short scripture centered on a protective incantation associated with the wrathful guardian deity Mahākāla. It is set soon after the Buddha's awakening, while he is still dwelling at the foot of the tree of awakening, having subdued…

item.title: The Noble Dhāraṇī of Mahākāla That Brings Liberation from All Fevers (Toh 1086)
item.description: The Noble Dhāraṇī of Mahākāla That Brings Liberation from All Fevers, known in Tibetan as Pakpa Nakpo Chenpö Zung Rimné Tamché Lé Tarwar Jepa, is a brief protective incantation addressed to Mahākāla, the Great Black One, a fierce guardian deity. After paying homage to all buddhas and bodhisattvas, the text introduces the dhāraṇī as the spell of Mahākāla, described as a dark yellow figure with…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī of the Goddess Mahākālī (Toh 1087)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī of the Goddess Mahākālī, known in Sanskrit as Devī Mahākālī Nāma Dhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Lha mo nag mo chen mo'i gzungs, is a short scripture centered on a powerful protective incantation. It is set shortly after the Buddha's awakening, as he stays at the foot of the tree of awakening, when the goddess Mahākālī approaches him. She is described as Sovereign Lady of the Desire Realm…

item.title: The Hundred and Eight Names of Śrīdevī Kālī (Toh 1088)
item.description: The Hundred and Eight Names of Śrīdevī Kālī, known in Sanskrit as Śrīdevīkālīnāma Aṣṭaśataka and in Tibetan as Dpal lha mo nag mo'i mtshan brgya rtsa brgyad pa, is a short scripture of praise that sets out a litany of epithets for the fierce goddess Śrīdevī, also called Mahākālī. It opens on Vulture Peak Mountain, where the Buddha is teaching the true names to the bodhisattvas and the goddess…

item.title: The Praise by Śakra, Lord of the Gods (Toh 1089)
item.description: The Praise by Śakra, Lord of the Gods, known in Tibetan as Lha'i dbang po brgya byin gyis bstod pa, is a very brief verse hymn attributed to Śakra, the king of the gods also known as Indra. No Sanskrit title is preserved with it. In a few lines, it describes the suffering of saṃsāra across the three times, driven by attachment, aversion, and delusion, in which gods and asuras alike are shaped by…

item.title: Praise of the Mistress of Diseases (Toh 1090)
item.description: The Praise of the Mistress of Diseases, known in Tibetan as Nad kyi bdag mo la bstod pa, is a short devotional hymn addressed to a fierce goddess who presides over illness. Her iconography closely recalls the Indian smallpox goddess often called Śītalā, though no Sanskrit title is securely attested here. In vivid verse, the hymn describes her anointed with sesame oil, wearing a single braid and…

item.title: Homage to All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas (Toh 1070)
item.description: This brief text, Toh 1070 in the Kangyur, is known only by its opening words, a Sanskrit invocation beginning "namaḥ sarva," meaning "homage to all," and no fuller English, Sanskrit, or Tibetan title can be determined with confidence. It is a short mantra of praise addressed to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, saluting them as those whose higher knowledge has blossomed in every direction, and…

item.title: Blessing the Offerings with the Mantra Oṃ Sarva Tathāgata Pūjā Megha (Toh 1071)
item.description: This brief text, which may be called in English the Blessing of Offerings, consists of a single mantra and a one-line instruction. Its Tibetan wording ends with the phrase mchod pa byin gyis brlab bo, meaning "one blesses the offerings," and no separate Sanskrit title is evident. The mantra opens with oṃ sarva tathāgata, invoking all the tathāgatas, and seems to evoke clouds of offerings…

item.title: Dhāraṇī of the Clouds of Offerings (Toh 1072)
item.description: This brief text, Toh 1072 in the Kangyur, is a short dhāraṇī whose title is simply its opening mantra, beginning "namaḥ sarva buddha bodhisattvānāṃ." It is often described as a mantra for producing clouds of offerings, though no separate formal title in Sanskrit or Tibetan can be confidently determined. The text presents a single Sanskrit formula addressed to all buddhas and bodhisattvas and…

item.title: Toh 1073 (Toh 1073)
item.description: This brief work, catalogued as Toh 1073 in the Kangyur, is a short dhāraṇī, or incantation, whose Sanskrit-derived formula opens with homage to all buddhas and bodhisattvas and closes with the word svāhā. Its title is not clearly preserved in the source lines, but its content concerns devotional practice: it teaches that simply reciting this formula is equivalent to having made offerings to the…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī for Polishing the Jewel (Toh 1074)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī for Polishing the Jewel, known in Tibetan by a title along the lines of Rinpoche Darwé Zung, is a very brief ritual instruction that pairs a short mantra with a simple devotional act. After paying homage to the Three Jewels, it directs the practitioner to recite the mantra while polishing a jewel, imagining that a boundless rain of jeweled parasols, victory banners, and similar…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī of Circumambulation (Toh 1075)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī of Circumambulation, whose Sanskrit title is likely rendered as Pradakṣiṇadhāraṇī and whose Tibetan title refers to circumambulation, is a very brief dhāraṇī text in the Kangyur, catalogued as Toh 1075. It opens with homage to the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, the buddha whose name means "Jewel Banner," and then presents a short incantation invoking him through repeated evocations of the…

item.title: The Noble Dhāraṇī for Circumambulating the Supports of the Jewels (Toh 1076)
item.description: The Noble Dhāraṇī for Circumambulating the Supports of the Jewels, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya Pradakṣāratnatrayā Nāma Dhāraṇī, is a very brief incantation text that also closes under the simpler name The Dhāraṇī of Circumambulation. After a homage to the Buddha Śākyamuni, it presents a single short mantra addressed to the Three Jewels of the ten directions and the three times, calling for…

item.title: The Essence of the Meteor of Wisdom (Toh 1077)
item.description: The Essence of the Meteor of Wisdom, whose Tibetan title would be rendered along the lines of Yeshé Karda Nyingpo and whose Sanskrit name may be reconstructed as something like Jñānolkāhṛdaya, is a brief ritual text centered on a single mantra. After paying homage to the Three Jewels and giving the mantra, it instructs the practitioner to sit beside a flowing stream or a lake, recite the mantra…

item.title: The Dhāraṇī Called Surūpa (Toh 1078)
item.description: The Dhāraṇī Called Surūpa, known in Sanskrit as the Surūpanāmadhāraṇī and in Tibetan as Su ru pa zhes bya ba'i gzungs, is a brief ritual text centered on a dhāraṇī, a sacred incantation addressed to the Tathāgata Surūpa, whose name means "Beautiful Form." After a homage to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, it presents the incantation and gives simple instructions for an offering to hungry ghosts…

item.title: The Torma Ritual for Bringing Relief to the Pretī Jvālāmukhī (Toh 1079)
item.description: The Torma Ritual for Bringing Relief to the Pretī Jvālāmukhī, known in Tibetan as Yi dags mo kha 'bar ma dbugs dbyung ba'i gtor ma'i cho ga, is a short ritual scripture concerning offerings made to hungry ghosts, or pretas. It opens with the Buddha teaching at the Nyagrodha Park near Kapilavastu, where Ānanda, meditating alone late at night, is visited by the pretī Jvālāmukhī, whose name means…

item.title: The Hevajra Sādhana Called The Treasury of Purity (Toh 1244)
item.description: The Means of Accomplishing Hevajra called The Treasury of Purity, in Sanskrit Viśuddhanidhi nāma Hevajrasādhana and in Tibetan Kyé Dorjé Drubpé Tap Nampar Dakpé Ter, is Toh 1244 in the Tengyur, where it belongs to the section of tantra commentaries. It is a sādhana, a ritual manual for meditative practice on Hevajra, the blue, eight-faced, sixteen-armed deity embraced by his consort Nairātmyā and…

item.title: The Means of Accomplishment Called Dispelling Delusion (Toh 1245)
item.description: The Means of Accomplishment called Dispelling Delusion, in Sanskrit Bhramahāra Sādhana and in Tibetan Trulpa Pongwa Zhejawé Druppé Tap, is a short Indian tantric practice manual, or sādhana, devoted to the deity Hevajra in his eight-faced, sixteen-armed, four-legged form as Heruka. Composed by the Indian master Ratnākaraśānti, it guides the mantra practitioner through a full day of practice…

item.title: The Torma Rite of Hevajra (Toh 1288)
item.description: The Torma Rite of Hevajra, in Sanskrit Hevajra Baliṃta Vidhi and in Tibetan Kyé Dorjé Zhejawé Tormé Choga, is a brief Indian tantric ritual manual, written mostly in verse, on offering torma, the ritual cake, within the practice of the deity Hevajra. It sets out three tormas in turn: one for the deities of the great maṇḍala, one for the ḍākinīs they emanate, and one for the guardians of the…

item.title: The Benefits of the Hand Emblems (Toh 1289)
item.description: The Benefits of the Hand Emblems, in Tibetan Chaktsen gyi Penyön, is a short verse work on the symbolism of the attributes held in the hands of the tantric deity Hevajra, who is joined with his consort Nairātmyā and surrounded by eight ḍākinīs; no Sanskrit title is given. After paying homage, the author explains one emblem after another, such as the curved knife, the skull cup, the hand drum, the…

item.title: The Stages of the Great Drop (Toh 1290)
item.description: The Stages of the Great Drop, in Sanskrit Mahātilakakrama and in Tibetan Tiklé Chenpö Rimpa, is a short Indian verse treatise of completion-stage instruction in the Hevajra tradition, attributed in its colophon to the Indian preceptor Vilāsavajra. In four chapters it moves from the stage of abiding by nature, where the aggregates, elements and sacred sites are shown to be the deities and places…

item.title: The Means of Accomplishment of the Blessed Hevajra: The Stages of Clear Realization Called Thoroughly Illuminating the Meaning (Toh 1291)
item.description: The Means of Accomplishing the Blessed Hevajra, the Stages of Clear Realization Called Thoroughly Illuminating the Meaning, known in Sanskrit as the Bhagavad Hevajra Sādhana Abhisamaya Kramārtha Prasanna and in Tibetan as Chomden De Kyé Dorjé Drubpé Tab Ngönpar Tokpé Rimpa Dön Rabtu Salwa, is a short Indian ritual manual, or sādhana, for the meditative practice of Hevajra, a principal deity of…

item.title: The Means of Accomplishment of Glorious Hevajra (Toh 1292)
item.description: The Means of Accomplishment of Glorious Hevajra, in Sanskrit Śrī Hevajrasādhana and in Tibetan Dpal dgyes pa rdo rje'i sgrub thabs, is a short tantric practice manual, a sādhana, for the meditative realization of the deity Hevajra. Written largely in verse, it guides the practitioner from the preliminary offerings, refuge and the four immeasurables through meditation on emptiness, the…

item.title: The Illumination of Reality (Toh 1293)
item.description: The Illumination of Reality, known in Sanskrit as the Tattvāloka and in Tibetan as Dekho Nanyi kyi Nangwa, is an Indian commentary on the practice of Hevajra, the wrathful deity of the Hevajra Tantra, and it is Toh 1293 in the Tengyur, where it belongs to the section of tantra commentaries. It opens with homage to Hevajra and verses praising the dance of Heruka, then explains the meditation step…

item.title: The Stages of Putting Hevajra into Practice (Toh 1294)
item.description: The Stages of Putting Hevajra into Practice, known in Tibetan as Gyepa Dorjé Lak tu Langwé Rimpa and given a Sanskrit title along the lines of Hevajrasya Hastavyavahārakrama, is a ritual manual for the practice of Hevajra, the central deity of the Hevajra Tantra. It sets out in order the practitioner's own preparation and deity yoga, the rites of the maṇḍala, the bestowal of empowerment on…

item.title: The Rite of the Torma (Toh 1295)
item.description: The Rite of the Torma, in Sanskrit Balividhi and in Tibetan Tormé Choga, is a short tantric ritual manual for offering torma, the ritual cake, to all the bhūtas and other spirits, so that the harm done by obstructors is pacified and every rite can be accomplished. It guides the practitioner through purifying all phenomena with mantras, arising as one's chosen deity, inviting the gods, world…

item.title: The Rite of the Maṇḍala of Glorious Hevajra (Toh 1296)
item.description: The Rite of the Maṇḍala of Glorious Hevajra, in Sanskrit Śrī Hevajramaṇḍalavidhi and in Tibetan Pal Gyepa Dorjé Kyilkhor gyi Choga, is a concise tantric ritual manual for conferring the empowerments of Hevajra. It describes how the vajra master prepares the maṇḍala, vases, offerings and tormas, generates Hevajra and the eight Nairātmyā goddesses, and confers the vase, secret, wisdom knowledge and…

item.title: The Means of Accomplishing Sixteen-Armed Hevajra (Toh 1297)
item.description: The Means of Accomplishing Sixteen-Armed Hevajra, in Sanskrit Hevajraṣoḍaśabhujasādhana and in Tibetan Kyé Dorjé Chak Chudrukpé Druppé Tap, is a short sādhana, a manual of daily deity practice, centered on Hevajra in his form with eight faces and sixteen arms, embraced by his consort Nairātmyā. It guides the practitioner through the whole day, from rising at dawn, protection, offerings to the…

item.title: The Stages of the Torma of Glorious Hevajra (Toh 1298)
item.description: The Stages of the Torma of Glorious Hevajra, known in Sanskrit as the Śrī Hevajrabalikrama and in Tibetan as Pal Gyepé Dorjé Tormé Rimpa, is a short ritual manual for offering torma, consecrated ritual cakes, within the practice of the Hevajra Tantra. After paying homage to Heruka, it explains the purposes of the offering, from long life, health and prosperity to the averting of harm and the…

item.title: The Sequence of the Torma Rite (Toh 1299)
item.description: The Sequence of the Torma Rite, known in Sanskrit as Balikarmakrama and in Tibetan as Tormé Lé kyi Rimpa, is a short ritual manual in verse on the offering of torma, the ritual cakes presented to enlightened deities, Dharma protectors, ḍākinīs, direction guardians, nāgas and spirits. Opening with homage to Vajrasattva, it explains that the torma is given to complete the two accumulations of merit…

item.title: The Torma Rite for All Bhūtas (Toh 1300)
item.description: The Torma Rite for All Bhūtas, known in Sanskrit as Sarvabhūtabalividhi and in Tibetan as Jungpo Tamché kyi Tormé Choga, is a brief ritual manual for offering torma, ritual cakes, to the whole host of spirits so that beings may be protected from harmful forces and obstructing vināyakas. Written from the standpoint of the Hevajra practitioner, it guides the yogin to visualize three stacked…

item.title: The Means of Accomplishing Hevajra (Toh 1301)
item.description: The Means of Accomplishing Hevajra, known in Sanskrit as the Hevajra Sādhana and in Tibetan as Kyé Dorjé Druppé Tap, is a short ritual manual in verse for the meditative practice of Hevajra, the wrathful Blood-Drinker or Heruka of the Hevajra Tantra. Opening with homage to Heruka, it sets out who is qualified for the practice, namely one who holds the vows and has received the empowerments, and…

item.title: Instructions on the Means of Accomplishing Glorious Hevajra (Toh 1302)
item.description: Instructions on the Means of Accomplishing Glorious Hevajra, whose Sanskrit title is given as Śrī Hevajranāmasādhanopika and whose Tibetan title is Pal Kyé Dorjé Drubpé Tab kyi Men-ngak, is a short tantric meditation manual, or sādhana, for practicing the deity Hevajra together with his consort Nairātmyā. Its colophon names it the Sādhana of the Innate Hevajra and attributes it to the great…
